description: Dillahunty argues that rational belief tracks each person’s available evidence, so the same objectively true proposition may warrant belief for one person but not another.
critique: Strongest feature: Dillahunty sharply separates objective truth from person-relative rational warrant: God could exist, reveal himself convincingly to Knechtle, withhold comparable evidence from Dillahunty, and thereby rationally differentiate their beliefs. Principal limitation: This hypothetical demonstrates conceptual possibility, not either participant’s actual evidence, while leaving the evidential threshold distinguishing justified acceptance from irrational belief materially underdeveloped. Live burden: Dillahunty must identify which publicly assessable or privately accessible considerations justify withholding his belief, explain how conflicting revelations should be evaluated, and connect that account to his central reality test. Locked score: The 86 properly rewards exceptional calibration, inferential coherence, precise exposition, and relevant clarification while preserving an evidentiary discount because the example maps possible unequal access more convincingly than it establishes anyone’s actual warrant.
